results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
All 37 aligned summaries match the controlling idea of their spec paragraph, in spec order (p01-p37); the three callout units are page format and match nothing.

Two units were marked two_ideas. Introduction ¶2 states the thesis and the roadmap, as the spec declares for p02. Ten Dysfunctions ¶3 gives the two diagnostic questions applied to Corvane and maps the book's two failure patterns onto them; the mapping is declared in p11's evidence and serves the same diagnosis, so it is not a separate controlling idea.

Every unit ties to the supporting claim its section declares (S1 scene, why-output; S2 ten-dysfunctions; S3 key-outcomes, sources-disagree; S4 the three patterns; S3/S4 worked example; S1/S3 anti-patterns; S1/S4 AI). No unit is untraceable.

Each of the seven tables, the figure and the six quotations has a sentence saying what it shows. The usage table in the scene is read by the first sentence of the next section, as the spec declares. For the vanity-metric table and the four-measures table the explaining sentence comes before the table, not after; the reading is still given.
All 35 declared transition_in entries were read at their boundary; each opening sentence or phrase expresses the declared relationship and picks up the declared known information.
The introduction opens on the Corvane scenario with figures, bridges through the reader's experience, states a disputable claim and a roadmap; none of the weak patterns applies.
The conclusion does not open with 'in conclusion', does not end on a rephrased thesis alone and does not introduce a new subtopic; the hand-off to the next chapter is declared by the spec.

The synthesis bullet says what no single section says (every dysfunction lets something other than the customer's result decide or count; the three patterns put it back into goal, plan and review). The so-what is carried as actions by the checklist (who can do what afterwards, what the driver did for each shipped item, whether a review ever ended in 'remove') rather than as a statement; 'a shipped feature that moved nothing is a cost' is not restated in the conclusion.
The closing paragraph returns to the forty-one features of 2024 and names them as output with no outcome above it, twenty-six used by one customer each, as callback.to declares.

The cold reader predicted all eleven body sections in the spec's order, the fictional running case and Build What Matters as evidence (and inferred further sources from 'where the sources disagree'), and the plain, practical tone. All eight roadmap promises were predicted.

The probe reader named the Hamster Wheel (output over outcomes), noted the Feature Factory as the alternative if a customer request decided, and restated the goal as a customer outcome with customer, result, measure, baseline, target and date. This matches the expected answer.

Why Output Becomes the Goal ¶1 says chapter 2 used the same two words for a change to the organization (users were teams, output a finished reorganization), states that here the object is the product and the user the customer, and links to [[the-organization-as-a-product]].

Each sourced concept names its book and concept (build trap and sales-led: Perri, Escaping the Build Trap; ten dysfunctions, three themes, product-driven company, key customer and business outcome, delivering and extracting value, Counting House: Foster and Nerlikar, Build What Matters). The author's extensions are marked where they occur (the mechanism, the signs and theme assignment, the vanity-metric wording, the six-part goal, the pyramid as recorded in the author's checklist, the four-measure comparison, the cost judgement, the outcome review, the resolution of the disagreement) or in the takeaway (the two diagnostic questions).

Each of the three patterns names its user and a measure: rewrite (the leader who sets a team's goal and the team; share of team goals with all six parts), drivers (product leaders who set team goals; share of goals and roadmap items naming their driver), review (the leader who reviews a team's work; share of shipped items reviewed on the date set and the number changed or removed).

results.finding: Both flow readers could not tell how the three open rows rewritten in the first pattern relate to the seventeen open promises ('further' than what), and so whether the SMS notification that 'shipped on time' in ¶3 was one of the five contractual promises or the team's own choice.
